reviews.text: Visiting the Terracotta Army is an incredible experience, though it requires a bit of stamina. There are multiple pits to explore, so be ready to do a lot of walking. We spent about 3-4 hours wandering through the site. We opted for the audio guide, which was decent and provided good context, but if you want the full story and hidden details, hiring an official guide on-site is probably the best way to go. As expected for such an iconic landmark, it was quite crowded, but the scale of the pits is so massive that it's still worth every minute. Definitely a bucket-list item!

Get ready to do a lot of walking! There are multiple buildings with things to look at. Watch out for scammers offering guided tours and pushing you to buy overpriced souvenirs. It is awesome to see! We went without a guide and just wandered at our own pace to look at everything. We spent probably around 3 hours looking around. We went with a chinese friend. I don't know why, but we didn't need tickets to get it, we just needed our passports. It was very crowded despite it being winter. So be careful of the crowds, as it can be easy to get lost in the crowd, especially kids.

Visited on a Tuesday around 3 pm and was told we were lucky—it wasn’t too busy, though still quite a few people around. I can only imagine how packed it gets during peak hours, so I’d definitely recommend that time slot if you’re looking for a more relaxed experience. The site itself is incredible—just like what you see in documentaries or YouTube videos, but even more impressive in person. We opted for a guided tour (about USD $20), and it was absolutely worth it. Our guide gave a rich, detailed overview of the history and zipped us through key areas like VIPs, making the whole visit smoother and more engaging. Highly recommend getting a guide—it elevated the entire experience. A brilliant, must-see destination if you’re in Xi’an.

Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum (秦始皇帝陵博物院) — A Must-Visit, Truly the 8th Wonder Visiting the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum is nothing short of breathtaking. This extraordinary site, often called the “8th Wonder of the World,” lives up to every bit of its reputation and more. Standing before the Terracotta Army, you immediately feel the weight of history, ingenuity, and ambition that shaped China over 2,000 years ago. The sheer scale and craftsmanship are astonishing—thousands of life-sized warriors, each with unique facial features, expressions, and armor, silently guarding China’s first emperor in perfect formation. It’s humbling to realize that these figures were created without modern technology, yet display remarkable realism and artistic sophistication. The museum itself is well organized and informative, with clear exhibits that guide visitors through the history of the Qin Dynasty, the unification of China, and the incredible archaeological discoveries made at the site. Walking through the massive pits, especially Pit 1, is an unforgettable experience that leaves you in awe of ancient engineering and vision. Beyond the Terracotta Army, the surrounding mausoleum area adds depth to the visit, helping you appreciate the emperor’s grand plan for the afterlife and his lasting impact on Chinese civilization. The site is spacious, well maintained, and thoughtfully designed for visitors from around the world. This is not just a museum—it is a journey back in time, a powerful reminder of human creativity and ambition on a monumental scale. Whether you’re a history lover or a first-time visitor to China, the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum is an absolute must-visit and truly deserving of its title as a tremendous 8th wonder of the world.

The Terracotta Warriors Museum is an absolute must-see when visiting Xi’an and one of the most important archaeological discoveries in the world. It is located just outside the city and is easy to reach by taxi or private transfer. The museum is spread across three main large exhibition halls, each housing a different section of the Terracotta Army. Each building showcases a unique collection of warriors, horses, chariots, and artifacts, and together they give you a powerful sense of the sheer scale and ambition behind this site. The Terracotta Warriors were built around 210 BCE to guard Qin Shi Huang in the afterlife. After unifying China for the first time and ending centuries of warfare, the emperor believed he would need the same military power in death as he had in life. Thousands of life-sized soldiers were buried in battle formation, each with distinct facial features, armor, and rank, believed to be modeled on real people. This level of detail, combined with advanced bronze weaponry and early mass-production techniques, shows just how sophisticated the Qin Dynasty was over 2,000 years ago. One important tip: do not pay for an on-site guide. You will be approached constantly, but it is unnecessary. The signage inside the museum is clear, and if you take the time to learn the history beforehand, you will get far more out of the visit. Understanding the significance of the Qin Dynasty and the emperor’s vision makes the experience far more meaningful than listening to rushed or generic explanations. Buy your ticket in advance on Trip.com to avoid queues and make entry smoother, especially during busy periods. This is a powerful and humbling place that was never meant to be seen, remaining buried for over 2,000 years until its discovery in 1974. Go prepared, take your time, skip the unnecessary extras, and let the scale and history of the site speak for itself.

This is just an amazing bit of Chinese history. Highly recommend. I went with a tour guide and would suggest this to anyone. The only thing is, prepare for crowds and a little of pushing and shoving. Especially in pit 1.

I was lucky enough to be here at the same time as the farmer that discovered this site, and was able to get a book with his autograph. How amazing to have found something so profound. It's overwhelming once you see the technical skill involved in creating every single one of them. I took home some mini replicas so I can enjoy them for years to come, though I'd love to visit again.

Interesting and well maintained exhibit. There are plenty of toilet for tourist and place kept clean. I recommend follow tour so you get knowledgeable tour guide to explain and provide historical background. As I understand the site was started 50 years ago, it was formerly a poor village, who now works for the deceased emperor , guiding and maintaining his museleum 2000 years after his death.
It’s must if you are near. Huge museum, lot of information. If you don’t have much time, don’t take guide. There are a lot of them in front of you of entrance and they are annoying. Enjoy your visit.
For those who love history, this place is interesting to visit. It was large and beautiful place. Avoid public holiday. Too crowded😔. You cannot enjoy the scenery and read the information

Must visit place. Colossal scale terracotta warriors pits are very impressive. Very well run. Use Tram cars to reduce walking from entrance to pits. Recommend engaging a guide to fill in the history behind the awe inspiring displays. English speaking guides available. 3 pits opened for display, pit 1 has the most terracotta warriors unearth and displayed. Ticket include visit to Li Garden. Main attraction are scale model of 2 chariots on display. Supposedly made of gold. Very intricate. Worth visiting. Guide introduced us to a VR Interactive display and Warrior Reborn Show. Both require additional ticket charges. We chose the Warrior Reborn Show. Interesting show as spectators were guided to move between scenes setups. Advisable to reserve one whole day for this place. Plan to visit during the off peak season like we did.

A must-visit landmark in Xi’an — the world-famous Terracotta Warriors site. You can easily take a Didi ride from downtown Xi’an for around 100 RMB. It’s highly recommended to book your entrance ticket in advance to avoid confusion at the gate, especially for foreign visitors. Official guides are available right at the entrance and can greatly enhance your visit with detailed historical explanations. Inside, you’ll find three main excavation pits open to visitors, along with a museum showcasing ancient weapons and artifacts discovered at the site. After finishing the tour, you’ll pass through a lively food street — perfect for lunch — before continuing to nearby Lishan Mountain, believed to be the actual tomb area of Emperor Qin Shi Huang. Plan about 1–2 hours for the visit. It’s an unforgettable experience that perfectly combines history, culture, and the legacy of China’s first emperor.

This was on my bucket list, and I think I built it up on my head too much that I was a bit disappointed when I got there. I imagined a lot more soldiers and getting closer to them to see the individual details of each statue. There were a few good specimens on display but it was of course incredibly busy so hard to spend any time appreciating them beyond a quick look and a photo. Still happy I went and have seen it, the story of the emperor they're guarding is also interesting.

Visiting the Terracotta Army is one of the most impressive experiences in China. Seeing thousands of clay warriors — each with unique facial features and details — is absolutely breathtaking. The site is well organized, with clear signs and a smooth visitor route. It’s best to come early in the morning to avoid the big crowds. Tickets can be bought online, and there’s a free shuttle bus between the entrance and the main hall. You can also see exhibitions and reconstructions showing how the army was discovered. Overall, it’s a fascinating and unforgettable place — definitely worth visiting at least once in your lifetime.

Standing before the Terracotta Army feels unreal. This vast underground army was created over 2,200 years ago to guard China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife. Discovered by local farmers in 1974, it remains one of the greatest archaeological finds in human history. Each soldier was buried facing east, as if ready to defend the empire forever. What makes it even more mind-blowing is that no two warriors are exactly the same. From facial expressions and hairstyles to armor and ranks, every figure shows incredible craftsmanship. There are infantry soldiers, archers, generals, horses, and chariots — once brightly painted, though most of the colors faded over time. Experts estimate there are over 8,000 soldiers, yet many pits are still unexcavated. Seeing it in person really hits different. Photos don’t fully capture the scale, the silence, and the weight of history here. This wasn’t just a tomb — it was a statement of power, belief, and immortality. A reminder that even after two millennia, the legacy of the Qin Dynasty still stands strong beneath the soil of Xi’an.

Specialised tour guides will bring you around the museum, the content is extremely detailed and very clear. The exhibits are extremely interesting and alot of information is available. Older exhibits that used to be on display at Pit 2 (the 4 horses and chariot) were removed during Covid and are still currently in storage. Not too sure when they will be re-exhibited. The place is incredible and its best to book tickets early or go with a tour group since it can get incredibly crowded.

Needless to explain the significance of the renowned Terracotta Army (兵马俑). Not only is it a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it is also considered one of the Eight Wonders of the World. There are three excavation pits, with Pit 1 being the largest and most extensively excavated. It truly showcases the sheer scale and grandeur of the army. Pit 2 is largely unexcavated, which is actually a great idea as it gives visitors a clear visual sense of what the site originally looked like - statues buried in soil, many of them broken into pieces. Pit 3 is much smaller and appears to be mostly excavated; it is believed to have served as the command or headquarters area of the army. I’m glad I brought my kids to see this significant historical site. Although they are still young, exposing them to such an important piece of history is a valuable educational experience - provided you are patient enough to explain things along the way. A cautionary note: the site is about 40 minutes from Xi’an city by ride-hailing apps such as DiDi. The shops around the perimeter close fairly early (around 6 pm), and it gets dark quite quickly. We had to make several attempts to hail a DiDi ride back to the city, as we did not feel comfortable randomly hopping into taxis on the street - many drivers were aggressively trying to persuade visitors to get into their cars. My advice: book or plan your return trip in advance.

Entrance tickets includes the 3 main pits of Terracotta Warriors and entrance to Lishan Garden where the bronze chariots are located. Lishan garden park is humongous so it's advisable to pay for the shuttle bus at the park entrance to visit the few pits inside. Great experience to see artifacts from thousands of years ago and to see their conservation efforts.

Seeing these magnificent statues in person, after years of only encountering them in history books, was an absolutely unforgettable experience. This is a fantastic museum and an absolute must-see for anyone visiting the area. Truly a historical marvel! ​We were fortunate to have a fantastic tour guide who enhanced the visit immensely. She not only provided us with amazing historical facts but also entertained us with funny, relevant stories, making the experience both educational and highly engaging.

A must-visit historical site in China. The site is large and the actual museum is far from the ticket entrance, so advisable to buy the electric buggy tickets (additional cost per person) if travelling with seniors, kids or just unable to walk too far. Tickets can be purchased at the entrance but you will be hounded by tons of tour guides charging few hundred yuan to be your guide once inside. You can rent an English audio guide for 40yuan (if i remember correctly) after entering instead. After touring the 3 pits, you are forced to exit through a maze of restaurants and shops - another unnecessarily long walk. Once you finally reach the entrance again, you can queue up for a bus to take you 1.5km to the mausoleum site, where it is just a few more uncovered pits. This is another huge site, and you have to pay for another electric car buggy to bring you around because it is quite impossible to walk when you are already so tired! Once we got off the buggy at the first stop, we were told we must follow one direction (flow) from the first stop to the last stop and are not allowed to turn back if we missed anything. This was told to us in Chinese... so Im not sure if foreigners would have been informed of this seemingly important instruction. The actual tomb of the emperor is not yet open. So this site is really just giving some history of the site, some other uncovered pits featuring horses and bronze charriots, and a very large museum showcasing how they made the statues and figurines in the olden days. Overall, the site could have used a lot more signages to guide us in the right direction. Felt a bit annoyed having to pay for the electric buggy on top of the already expensive ticket fees at two sites.

This is well known and is a UNESCO World Heritage and became designated in 1987 due to its exceptional artistic quality and historical value. Archaeologists estimate there are over 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots, and 670 horses, though thousands remain unexcavated to avoid damage. The story is now well known with this massive collection of life-sized clay sculptures depicting the armies of Qin Shi Huang, the first Emperor of China. They were buried with the Emperor around 210–209 BCE and were his "silent army" was intended to protect him in the afterlife. I am not sure how that went! However it is part of one of the largest and most elaborate mausoleums ever constructed. There must have been a lot of work put into the sculptures as no two figures are identical with each warrior possessing distinct facial features, expressions, hairstyles, and clothing according to their rank. Despite its enormous size it seems to have got lost in memory as the entire army was discovered in March 1974 by local farmers digging a well near Xi'an, Shaanxi province. The place is located about 35–40 km northeast of the city center of Xi'an.

It’s been on my must visit places for years. And finally got to see it and it was stunning! The magnitude of the site and the 8000 status were incredible. Each soldier was uniquely carved and so human like. The rich culture and history behind the side and the discover of it all were unforgettable!

This is my 2nd visit in 2 consecutive years and I still feel excited about it. This time I have different official guide lady telling me other side stories of the Emperor Qin which changes my perspective view on life and human behaviour. It is truly an experience that I would never forget.

I can honestly say that visiting the Terracotta Army was an overwhelming and deeply moving experience. The sheer scale of this place is something photos and documentaries simply cannot capture—you have to see it with your own eyes. I was utterly amazed and profoundly glad I made this trip; it truly is worth the once-in-a-lifetime effort. The Pit 1 (The Infantry): This is the main attraction and where the breathtaking scale hits you. Seeing thousands of life-sized soldiers, chariots, and horses lined up in ancient battle formation, guarding the First Emperor for over two millennia of the Qin Dynasty, is just jaw-dropping. I was amazed by the Bronze Chariots. The intricate detail and preservation of these half-scale pieces are often called the "Crown of Bronzes" for a reason. Warning: The site is huge and popular, so try to arrive early to beat the biggest crowds, I will recommend consider hiring an audio guide to truly appreciate the historical context.

Very popular attraction. But the crowds are manageable. I don't reccomend going with a tour as it is easy to navigate and the history is straight forward. The tour we booked through klook was a scam. They kept trying to sell us things . Don't fall for the fake 'farmer' who found the terracotta army. Or the fake jade experience. Or the mausoleum XR experience. The bad tours will try to sell you terracotta warriors souvenirs that were apparently dug from same site.

Amazing artwork eveywhere. The best place to buy clay soliders is in the back in a at shop that was kinda hidden from the front shops. They sell life size replicas and all the other smaller sizes. Skip the tourist shops at the front selling plastic. One shop owner even gave them me a pottery factory tour after buying a statue. Once in a lifetime experience . I loved it!

A fantastic day! You will need at least 2.5hours inside the exhibition complex to absorb the wonder and glory of the terracotta warriors! The mausoleum is 50 mins away from the city centre - we took a didi and it was around USD15 one way. There are 3 pits to enjoy along with a host of displays, just like a museum. Food choices are plenty and toilets are aplenty

Truly amazing. This is another site, separated a little away, from the Terracota Army museum. This site has 3 exhibition halls and one of them has the amazing ancient bronze chariots. The emperor's tomb has not been opened.

Very impressive place to see the uncovered terracotta soldiers. When you visit, look at the details on some of the life sized exhibits. You can see lines on the palms, details on individual hairstyles, etc.. Excavation and restoration continue to happen. There are 3 main buildings to visit within the same compound. On rainy days, make sure you have umbrellas or raincoats as the monsoon rains can be quite hard and relentless. They have a shop that sells replicas of terracotta soldiers with certificates showing they were made from the same clay as the originals. Above the shop is a restaurant that serves traditional Chinese food. Public toilets are scattered all over the place so very convenient.

Astounding site, very well done. This will hit harder if you have a good guide to explain the history and how the warriors were made and the life of the emperor, etc. It is always very crowded in the main building, so save it for the very end of the day or go right as they first open.

Forget “Terracotta Army.” The proper name is Emperor Qin Shi Huang’s Mausoleum, a title that screams “I refuse to die quietly.” The first emperor of China didn’t settle for a tomb—he built an underground empire staffed by thousands of clay soldiers, because apparently ruling the living wasn’t enough. You walk in with a crowd large enough to start a small riot, instantly surrounded by more security than an airport on red alert. Guards everywhere, watching like hawks. Blink wrong and they’ll assume you’re plotting a terracotta heist. The soldiers themselves? Unreal. Every single one has a different face, hairstyle, even expression, and they look ready to march off the second someone invents Wi-Fi for clay. But here’s the kicker: most of them are still buried, sealed underground in perfect formation, waiting for the sequel no one dares to dig up yet. Then comes the exit. You’d think after paying respects to an emperor’s eternal army, you’d get a quiet walk back to the bus. Nope. You get a shopping complex the size of a small planet. Souvenirs, snacks, T-shirts, fake soldiers, real capitalism. The afterlife apparently comes with a food court now. You can’t touch anything, you can’t get too close, but you’ll still leave impressed as hell and slightly poorer. 5 out of 5. The most epic graveyard in human history, followed by the most shameless gift shop ever built.

It's a marvel of mankind to create. What a magnificent place this is! The Terracotta Army look so formidable, each of Terracotta Warriors is unique in shape, face, skin color, and structure. Many millions of tourists visit this place in a year Don’t miss it. You should definitely visit at least once in your life.

A stunning site where this army was discovered. I recommend going with a guide and avoiding peak hours. I also advise against going there in the height of summer, as you will find rivers of people and you will not enjoy the visit at all. I recommend a stick for taking photos and videos with your phone.

A must when you are in Xi'an. The terracotta army/warriors is dispatched in pits. Most of the warriors are in pit 1. You will see them from a balcony a little far away. The place is overcrowded and some people will be pushy to have access to the first row of visitors. My suggestion : walk a little to the side - right or left - and you will see better. The Terracotta army is unique in the world and definitely worth a visit despite the queue and the time you will have to wait to have access to the site. However, the number of visitors should be limited in a closed setting. I was in a small group with a Tour Operator, so I didn't get the inconveniences mentioned by some tourists.

Visiting Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum to see the Terracotta Army is undeniably a great opportunity to see one of the world's most important archaeological discoveries. I have always wanted to witness this historical marvel firsthand, and the sheer scale and intricate detail of the warriors truly are awe-inspiring. It is an incredible testament to ancient craftsmanship and imperial power. However, my experience was definitely shaped by the elements. The brutal 104 F heat made the visit incredibly challenging. Walking between the various pits and exhibition halls under such intense sun, even with water, was quite draining. It certainly detracted from my ability to fully immerse myself in the historical significance of the site, as I was constantly seeking shade and a cooler spot. I strongly advise future visitors to check the weather and consider cooler months if possible. Beyond the heat, the museum experience was typical for a major attraction in China, complete with massive crowds and queues. Navigating through the throngs of people to get a good view of the pits required patience and some strategic positioning. While the sheer number of visitors speaks to the site's popularity, it does mean that a serene, contemplative experience is hard to come by. I found myself waiting in lines for entry and to move between viewing areas. Despite these challenges, seeing the Terracotta Army remains an unforgettable experience. It is a powerful historical site that every traveler should try to visit. Just be prepared for the heat, the crowds, and the typical museum flow you might encounter at such a popular destination.

Amazing. Truly amazing if you consider all the terracotta soldiers were made 2270 years ago. It was great to see history in front of you. Be aware of the hawkers. The box of 5 terracotta soldiers??? Pay no more than 50 Yuan...as little as 20. Don't pay in euro or aud.

An absolutely unforgettable site! As someone passionate about Chinese history and culture, visiting the Terracotta Army had been a dream of mine, and I was not disappointed when I finally went in September 2024. The site is vast and full of incredible details to discover. What fascinated me most was seeing that each statue is unique, with its own features and expressions, making the whole army feel so alive and impressive. Make sure to allow enough time to explore everything. A must-see when visiting Xi’an!

It is always worth the visit. Be prepared for the crowd. The best time to enter is 8:30. Crowd arrives later. Take official translator/guide. Do not get hunted by predators outside the entrance. Climb the path for 15 minutes until the pits. If you need the shuttle you may have to wait a while. Have your passport ready. You will need it twice. Once at the main entrance, and later after arriving at the pits. You may want start with pit #1 and go to pit #3 and finish with pit #2. You will walk over the pit #4, which was excavated and filled in and covered later on. The guide will tell you the stories. The mound (where the mausoleum is thought to be) is worth a visit in good weather. It is another 15 minutes walk from the pits. But there are no excavated areas there. Over 60 pits have been excavated but only three are open to visitors. The two chariots previously in the local museum near the entrance/exit are now in Xian city.

Terracotta army. its impressive, sure, but also a little underwhelming in my opinion. For a 2 hour ride from xi'an, dealing with a bunch of tourists, and for only a portion of the army actually being uncovered, seems underwhelming for me. That being said however, im not very well versed in the history of the mausoleum (or with the qin empire in general) so maybe with some more cultural context, it could be a better experience

This is it - the Eighth Wonder of the World. An amazing experience to be here and to learn about the history and archeological work involved. Pit Number One is, of course, the best known and where the greatest excavation has taken place, but the other three are each also fascinating.

This historical monument in China is a stark reminder how a superstitious Emperor could marshal an entire economy to build an elaborated Royal Tomb for his afterlife! There are probably untold story of actual human ritual sacrifices as well to accompany the Emperor. At less the military man were mostly spared in fear of a coup or revolt. Which is probably why we see only Clay Terracotta warriors and not one filled with human corpses. A must visit if you are in 西安. Local tourism get a great boost from the huge number of visitor even during low season.

Spectacular & must visit with a guide to explain. Came during off peak and the place was already packed. Hard to imagine how it would be like during peak period. Be sure not to lose Your guide as reception was not good inside. Overall good experience except that if you come with a guide it will be rushed. After the tour you may choose to go back to the pits on your own again to take more pictures.
3 different building site housing the finds plus a museum.Excavation still on going as very delicate operation.Worth a visit with a guide.

Beautiful place with amazing history! Would recommend to buy tickets in advance and maby get a guide because it can be difficult to navigate through the big areas. Also important to notice is, that the bus who brings you to the digging sites is outside the museum area and near the entrance.
Emperor Qin wanted protection in the afterlife so he had artisans from local and afar create over 6000 individual terracotta soldiers for his army.

A must visit place with three pits and a museum, the whole area is well built with great atmosphere, mountains and clouds are also great view. You can see those warriors in great details and to know the process of the archaeological process and history. A few drawbacks: 1. Way too crowded at the time of my visit, at around 2pm every pit has already filled with people and somehow no one bother to queue and just push each other to get a better view. 2. The transportation to the Xi’an city is not very convenient, if take public transportation might need to transfer between bus and subway and there is no clear sign of where is the station. Better not take the round trip on those bus at buses around the Bell tower station, as they will not departure at the agreed time and bring you to visit some newly build theme attractions to charge you more. Even if you refuse to visit, you still need to wait for everyone to take the returning bus which will usually 1-2 hours late than the agreed returning time. Besides, on the bus the guide will speak non-stop with microphone to urge you participate in those charged event and the driver intentionally drive slower to let the guide speak more. 3. Foreigner better double check the ticket you bought, met many foreigners bought ticket from trip.com or pay with foreign cards cannot enter and have to waste time to get a paper ticket at the sales office.

It was super hot, but the experience was worth it in my opinion. There are 3 Pits where you can see the Warriors, which look amazing. There is also a museum. The buildings HAVE AC, but it is pretty crowded especially when there are groups with guides.
Everyone comes to Xian to see the Terracotta warriors or the locals are in dress up cos play. 2000+ years of history. The Chinese guided tours are very affordable.

This being one of the most famous and important archeological sites in the world, is treated as the national treasure as it is. This is the burial location and after life preparation for the first emperor of China. The Qin dynasty. This is a must see if in the region and tickets should be bought in advance to ensure entry. There are audio guides you can rent in many languages but they are a bit spotty. There are guides outside of the enterance that charge as guides but I do not know their prices. Maybe, being the time of the year, the crowds were insane. (Weekend visit and on summer holiday.) That being said, I've heard that it gets pretty busy during off season times too. The staff will herd you through the site in a specific order and discourage back tracking. They have a gift shot that is fairly expensive and officials and guides are somewhat pushy to get you to buy more. Be willing to walk away and they can give you a discount. Some guys will sell stone statues in the crowds....they are worth a look, often less expensive than the shops. You have to see these works of art but be ready to fight for photo space.

You cannot miss this ... really, it is sensational. The pits where the terracotta warriors are excavated (an ongoing process) are vast, covered by several halls. The museum goes into more detail, and has the advantage of being less crowded. Being jostled by the masses of visitors (most are domestic tourists) can feel claustrophobic, but if you go with the flow you should be fine. And, if in doubt, gently push your way forward.

Genuinely impressive to see what work has been put in this in former times. The excavations can be den from pretty close, so drystone of the soldiers can be observed pretty well. The site stretches over three big halls. There's also a museum showing other artefacts and explaining how everything was built. Expect a lot of tourists especially in weekends and holidays. It can be very crowded in the main hall, for the rest it gets better. Buying tickets in advance is smart. It is possible to get them in site but it's unnecessary waiting. Behind the exit the way back to the parking lot is through a food street, so you don't have to go hungry. Since the site is quite a bit outside the city, consider taking a driver for the day.
Great experience and well laid out. Would definitely do the old city behind the pits as well. Easy to get their via public transport.

I visited on Saturday 13 Sept 2025. There were thousands of people. My advice is to arrive as early as possible - it is about 70 km from Xi'an. It was very interesting to see all the warriors,horses and other objects on display, and to read about the history and background.
For any visitor exploring Xi’an, this museum is a must, highly recommended. Very popular, lots of people.

What more needs to be said about one of the greatest archaeological discoveries of all time. An incredible sight to see. It does get busy so advise to head there very first thing before the tour buses arrive. Also make sure you don't miss the free shuttle bus to the mausoleum and tomb complex which is about 1.5km away. Many foreigners miss this and don't see the main site of the actual tomb or the chariot museum which is actually the most modern and best explained museum in the whole complex.
Historical place, they made every statue of terracotta warriors different. Amazing

Its a really special and unique place. If your going near Xi'an its a must. The bad thing about it is how crowded it is. People push forward and will touch you. It was also really hot when I went and the drinks are alot more expensive then else where. Still its such an awesome place to go and its amazing to see how much effort is done in making the army. With details and the history about it is what makes it such an cool expierience.
No visit to Xi'an is complete without taking this in. Easy to reach by rideshare ("Didi") and we'll work the effort.

This was high on my must see, must go list. Xi'an is a busy and beautiful city to see and enjoy. The Terracotta Warriors was the highlight of this trip. It was amazing to see this incredible find. I stayed at the Westin Hotel, which is also across the street from the Flying Goose Pagoda. Worthy note, avoid going in the heat of the summer, if possible. Like and follow for more amazing places to see and visit around the world

When you arrive here your come to a big square with loads of tour guides (many speak basic English), and tour groups who will sort everything out for you. There was plenty to see, and you can take your time to work through it. The site is amazing. There are food courts. And a market of surviver, the market is full of pests trying to sell you things. At the end your come to a bus and taxi area, and the taxis are pests too.

This has to be the 8th wonder of the world. It's simply unreal and such an incredible excavation job that is ongoing. It will take your breath away. Nice touch to meet the founder Mr Yang's brother at the family store and get a personal touch of how it came to be

Visiting the Terracotta Army is a must-do in Xi’an, but honestly, it felt a bit underwhelming. There are just three main buildings to explore, and while the history is fascinating, the overall experience didn’t quite live up to the hype. After finishing the exhibits, the exit route takes you through a long stretch of outdoor malls and souvenir shops, which felt more commercialized than immersive. One thing that annoyed me was the pushy tourist guides constantly offering their services. Some were really persistent, and I had to be firm in turning them down. You don’t need them—just bring your passport and buy the ticket yourself! No need to trust these guides claiming they can "help" you. The walk to the main area was a bit long, but since it was snowing heavily, I didn’t mind at all. The cold, snowy atmosphere made everything feel magical, and it was honestly my happiest moment in Xi’an. The 1+ hour Didi ride didn’t feel worth it for the site itself, but the snow made the entire trip unforgettable!

Our second visit and this time with an English speaking guide. She appeared knowledgeable but know that the tour includes a stops to souvenir shops. Also a VR stop which was good, even if you don't understand Chinese you get the gist of what's explained.
Must visit. It is amazing to know how the ancient create the warriors that eventually tell stories of their times for generations. What a good way to keep history for future to remember forever.
Get here early, before the crowds, you'll need ID to buy a ticket and get in. It's well outside the city. If you love history it's a must, but it is probably why you came to Xi'an.

The Terracotta Army – pure awe when I first laid eyes on this monument! An incredible historical site, impressively preserved, that makes you feel the power and grandeur of ancient China. A must-see experience!

In Xi-an we visited the Terra Cotta mausoleum and museum which is the main attraction of the City. A must-visit place when visiting China. We also visited the old city and strolled over the wall around the city and through the muslim market; also very worthwhile. At night we went to the emperor's banquet and dance show. While the food was so so, the show was really magnificent.

Public Bus Route 306 (Line 5) for tourists: As of March 2025 the 306 does NOT go from Xi'an central railway station, but from Fangzhicheng metro station. At the metro station take exit A and upon reaching the outside main road, the 306 bus stop is located 100 metres to your right. The 306 buses are double-decker designs and it cost 5 Yuan each way. You do not need to wake up early and get there for 08:30 as various blogs state. 08:30 low season is the busiest time (though still not super busy). At 08:30 I arrived and the ticket counter had only 3 people queuing for physical tickets. The price is 120 Yuan and cards were accepted. Most tourists are Chinese tour groups and so all their tickets are pre-bought. At 08:30 there were approximately 2,000 people, though nobody was arriving when I left after 2 hours at 10:30, which would seem to be the perfect time to visit, or thereafter. 2 hours exactly was sufficient for all 3 pits and the "museum". The complex itself is very disappointing. The warriors are nevertheless worth seeing of course due to the uniqueness and consequent marvel they exhibit, but the actual site is beyond poor.The museum is 1/10. A joke. And the entire compound is dilapidated and abandoned in parts (even though they must be making hundreds of millions of dollars per year from ticket sales alone).

When I visited on 12 Sept 2025, the visit exceeded my expectations. The ɓuildings housing the excibitions where impressive. Thousands of people visit daily! The size and numbers of the warriors were larger than expected.

This is something special! It is breathtaking as it is humbling. Truly a masterpiece for the ages. I will not add to the story as it was told and retold - despite its definite allure - but I can offer a bit of advice: reserve in advance, stay away from the weekends and especially Chinese national holidays (check online for the yearly calendar - the crowds will be overwhelming) and go for the first possible entry window in the morning. Only without the crowds will the full beauty reveal itself. PS: I could not add this onto the map, but I wanted people to go and try it nonetheless: Xi'an is well - known for its colorful cuisine. One of these famous dishes is a "Persimmon pancake" or 柿子饼. Normally these pancakes would be made only of fried dough, but as luck would have it we found a small shop in a narrow alley away from the crowds, where honey filling was inserted into the fried pancake - result: an absolutely delicious sweet snack taken directly out of my dreams. I warmly suggest everyone to install Amap (a Chinese map app but in English - it will help you to navigate when in China in general) and insert the address below. It is located on the edge of the Muslim street area. Address of the persimmon pancake shop: 陕西省西安市莲湖区小学习巷79号 Name of the shop: 清真老贾家蜂蜜凉粽子 Enjoy! :D

It is amazing and magnificent, we gotten a local guide that speaks English but we could understand her better in mandarin. I feel we could do without guide because there is explanation board in both Chinese and English. Also the guide seems to rush us through and skip some artifacts. We spend almost a half a day to complete the terracotta pits and Qinshihuang’s Mausoleums.

100% worth the trip, it’s a miracle of human ingenuity from the past that is a once in a lifetime visit for most. I can’t recommend it enough. The scale is incredible. Try to find a guide in your own language, will really benefit from their experience. We found one while waiting around outside and she was great!

This was a once in a lifetime experience for us. I have seen a small example when they was on tour in Liverpool but nothing compares to seeing them in place absolutely outstanding experience. We hired a guide who sorted all our entries and tickets which I would advise. I would also advise going early as you can as this place is mad busy. Seeing the terracotta warriors and how the pits had been found and also previously burned was a great experience. The work that went into building these and now the work that is ongoing that is about preserving these items is massive. It is a colossal site took us around three hours to get around we show three pits which was well worth it. If you want good pics you need to be able to push your way ahead as nobody makes space for you but it is worth the effort. The grounds outside are also extremely well looked after as we found throughout our trip around China it is clean everywhere and this place was no exception. There are vending machines as expected but you will wechat or alipay i would recommend buying a 5g China mobile card for your trip as we did not we only had credit cards which are not accepted everywhere and also cash which is widely accepted just not by vending machines. It is a shop which you would expect but be prepared to haggle or over pay it is a hard sell start by cutting the price by 2 3rds and work up make them wait and don't be to keen.

One of the most magnificent places I have been to/things I have seen. It will only get better over time as well, as they are always finding/restoring more and more soldiers over time. Despite the crowds which can be overwhelming at times, it is still very worth the trip if traveling to or around Xi'an. It seems worth it to pay for a tour guide or at least do what we did, and get the audio guide. So much great information about the history and restoration efforts. One thing I have not seen people mention is the pomegranate juice stalls outside the grounds. We went last October which happened to be pomegranate season. So I cannot speak to the quality the rest of the year, but at that time, it was so fresh, possibly the best juice I have ever had. They generally have some juice bottles already sitting out, but you'll want them to freshly squeeze you a new one. So good we had to buy another round. I still think about how good that juice was even months later.

Lots of fun. Memorable experience and learned a lot. Had no idea idea that most if not all of the warriors were found destroyed since the ceiling had caved in and we're later reconstructed piece by piece! Also had no idea that there are a lot more that are still buried and left like that on purpose with the hope that eventually we will have the technology to unearth them without losing their color within a few minutes. We met with the farmer who found them and took a few photos. He's very nice.
Wanted to visit this place for a long time . Amazing! This complex is huge and lot to discover. Summer time it's extremely crowded . But we were there in December. It was moderate crowd .

Visiting in October good as not overcrowded, good temperature. You can buy tickets there, and easy enough with your passport. We didn't use a guide and didn't regret it - had read a bit about it before and some informative but limited signs - just the viewing was great. Pit 1 was the best (biggest most excavated) and the Museum was tops... but good to walk though It's 2 and 3. Happy days!
Definitely worth the visit but prepare for a lot of people (like always when in China)

History check with actual artifacts circa 220BC is always interesting. They have been trying to put together the shattered pieces for 46yrs. I'm told that about 1100 warriors have been restored as much as possible and another 8000 remain in waiting. The details on the warriors are very impressive. The sole markings of the archers, muscles in the arms, armours and ranking were all highly impressive. As of Jan2025, we visited a new display of artisans, acrobats and bronze birds from the latest excavation buried to entertain the Emperor Qin in the afterlife. We visited in the Jan winter. Queues were short and no crowds to taunt us. Brilliant!

Highly recommend visiting the Terracotta Warriors Museum. Amazing site where excavation is still being performed to uncover more relics. Visitors can easily see the terracotta relics, which can be crowded at times. Recommend waiting for crowds to pass to access good phototaking positions. There are several museum buildings. I like the smaller buildings, relics are better preserved, and crowds are spread out. The merchandise souvenir shops are expensive. Local restaurants and food stalls outside are fun and offer good value dishes. On certain days, you should meet the owner of the land and person who first discovered the terracotta warriors.
There are no words to describe this wonder of world's art and history. Nevertheless it is a very crowded place and you have to be quick to grab any free spot.

If you visit Xi’an in China, this is a place you simply must see. The awe-inspiring and endless Terracotta Army… Many clay figures are still buried, and each one is being excavated carefully with brushes. These excavation activities even take place in the exhibition area, where you can see archaeologists working. There’s a chance that in the future, direct viewing could be restricted, with only a few pieces displayed in a museum setting. If that happens, being able to view the site in person now will feel like a privilege. The scale is overwhelming, beyond what any photo or video can capture. Seeing the Terracotta Army in Xi’an feels like you’ve completed 70% of your journey. Wishing you a wonderful trip…

If you are in Xi'an, definitely you have to go to Terracota museum. It is about 1h drive from the city, you can take Didi which is kind of private transport. There is an option-public transport such a bus, but if you need to save time-recommend private option. Also I would recommend to buy the ticket entrance in advance.

A wonderful and amazing historical place in China. The relics are very carefully preserved and well maintained and the culture is beautifully shown to the whole world. It can be indeed regarded as World's 8th wonder with its uniqueness. The area was well maintained and spot clean. Beautiful and green mountains are near the tomb showing great beauty. Pakistan should also follow this presentations methods as there are also a lot of relics in Pakistan.

Immense hangars of terracotta Warriors and horses in various stages of repair, plus museum with video and lifesize warriors. Fabulous! In the photos here. You can also see workers in the process of repairing some.

What a fantastic trip back in time. The work being undertaken here is truly astounding. There is some flat walking to do and be prepared for a crowd. Conveniences and stores covered all never of needs.

Simply AMAZING! what a treat for something like this came from nearly 2300 years ago! This museum is well presented and preserved. I was so impressed with Xi’an’s rich in culture and history. Must visit 👍

What a spectacle, walking in to the main dig site, Pit 1, and coming face to face with the warriors it’s a site to behold, the sheer size and scale is something you can’t comprehend just by seeing images or shows or TV. You first see the reconstructed warriors and horses before moving along the pit and seeing the repair area. Pits 2 and 3 then have extra excavation areas with some more warriors and horses, their condition varies but they aren’t as good as Pit 1. The Exhibition Hall was the last stop, our group was lucky enough to be there during the 50th Anniversary of the discover of the Terracotta Warriors so there was an exhibition of the most colourful and well-preserved pieces. My advice would be to get there as early as possible before it gets too busy! The amount of visitors made it quite difficult to pass and view certain areas at times, especially the main site along with the best preserved areas, which are behind glass. The Terracotta Warriors was always something on my Bucket List and they beat all my expectations, I was blown away and remain impressed by Emperor Qin’s vision, how everything was constructed more than 2200 years ago and how the modern Chinese government is continuing to fund such a dig, and rightfully so. You will not regret going here at all! The only thing I would warn about, is the smell in the toilets, hold your nose.

Incredible experience, probably one of the most interesting things I've ever seen. There was a optional movie to start for 70rmb per person, was definitely worth it. Provided a good history lesson before the start of the official visit. Make sure to bring a passport. I don't know if there's a real need for going on an organized tour, most the information is on Google. You can enter and stay in the 3 halls as long as you want. Hall 2 is not very interesting. Hall 1 is the big one, and hall 3 is also very interesting.

This is without a doubt one of the most amazing and impressive archeological sights in the world! It's an absolute must see for anyone who is interested in the ancient world. Make sure you go to both the museum with the terracotta warriors and also the one with the bronzes which is up the hill a bit!
Terracotta Army, a place that definately gives you goosebumps. Do not depend thru documentary as you will never be able to feel that aura. A history and a must to visit when you are at Xi An, China

And don't waste too much time to fight the crowds to see the statue displays in pit 2, the artifact museum has plenty more on display and is generally less crowded.

Need to see with own eyes. Worth a visit just that not really friendly to non-Chinese speaking tourist. If you have a physical ticket, a ride on electric cart to the museum entrance is free. Else 5 Yuan per person.You can also walk. If booked in advance, just queue to enter the complex using your passport. Scan again to enter museum compound. Suggested first visit is Pit 1, the main excavation point. Then to exhibition hall. That's the main two if you are tired. If still have energy, go to Pit 2 and Pit 3.

Bucket list … there are no words, even though I’ll try to write some down. Whatever you had in your mind, whatever you’ve seen on TV, doesn’t even come close. You can just sit and stare at these amazing statues for hours, hopefully with a guide who is explaining everything to you. There are just rows and rows of warriors, each individually done and unique, and you can wander around for hours experiencing this marvel. Yes, crowds to be expected but it’s just incredible. 10/10 … highly recommend!

Great place and one to cross off the bucket list. They did find the site in 1974 and they are apparently still excavating, but it doesn't look like they've done much since the original lot. As it's still half excavated and they've built a load of buildings and a bit of a restaurant town around it lol. Anyway, definitely worth a visit. Really cool to see them in real life. All models are different from heights to faces.

The Terracotta Warriors in Xi'an are nothing short of awe-inspiring—a must-see destination that transports you back to the grandeur of ancient China. Standing face-to-face with thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, each with unique facial expressions and intricate details, is a surreal experience. The scale of the site is overwhelming, reflecting the immense ambition of Emperor Qin Shi Huang’s vision to protect his empire in the afterlife. The museum is well-organized, with informative exhibits that offer insights into the craftsmanship, history, and archaeological significance of the warriors. Whether you're a history buff or a casual traveler, witnessing this 2,000-year-old army firsthand is a truly unforgettable experience.

Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum is an awe-inspiring testament to ancient Chinese ingenuity and craftsmanship. The site, home to the famous Terracotta Army, offers a fascinating glimpse into the past with its life-sized statues that were meticulously crafted to guard the emperor in the afterlife. The scale and detail of the figures are breathtaking, and the surrounding museum provides valuable historical context. The mausoleum complex itself is well-preserved, and the guided tours are informative and engaging. This UNESCO World Heritage site is a must-visit for history enthusiasts and anyone interested in the grandeur of ancient China.

Incredible, spectacular history of ancient China. There are three museums altogether. These museums are so popular that there are always long queues. Recommend to visit as early as possible to avoid the huge crowds and to get the better position to see the worriers. The inside of the No. 1 museum getting quite hot during summer as there is no air conditioner.

This is place is amazing! The Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi'an, China is something you must see when visiting China. It's home to the famous Terracotta Army of thousands of life size clay sculptures, and is a wonder of the ancient world. It is the 3rd century BC tomb of imperial China’s first emperor. This was my 4th time visiting this active archaeological site in the last 25 years, but my kids first time and they loved it. This is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The site includes thousands of life-sized figures, chariots, and horses. Each figure has a unique facial expression and details. The discovery of the Terracotta Army in 1974 was one of the biggest archaeological discoveries of the 20th century . The museum complex is huge and you will need a few hours to see everything. It is well-organized, with three main pits that house the warriors. The site also offers information about the construction, burial practices, and the history of the Qin Dynasty. The museum can get crowded, especially during peak tourist seasons. We went in late November on a weekday, and while it was busy the crowds weren’t overwhelming.

During my trip to China, I finally visited a place I had heard about countless times in the news and movies. The site was packed with tourists, both Asians and non-Asians, making it quite crowded even during non-peak seasons. While the historical stories fascinated me, the actual physical view of the place left me feeling less awestruck than expected. Despite the crowds, the surrounding area was commercialized, but prices remained reasonable. If you're Asian, chances are you've encountered this place in media. I recommend a visit for the historical value, especially with a tour guide to delve into its stories. However, manage your expectations; it's a brief 1.5-hour visit. Personally, I don't plan on returning unless the tomb of the first emperor is excavated. Once was enough for me.

I took a train from Malaysia to Europe. Kunming was a transit city in my itinerary. Welcome to follow my YouTube channel [Lonely Railway Explorer] Malaysia to Europe series, also check the videos to know more about this museum. This wonder 8 museum is must visit in your life, but don't go on weekend or local public holiday. And please buy ticket online with explainer.

**Review of Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum (Terracotta Warriors)** A trip to Xi’an isn’t complete without visiting the Terracotta Warriors—this UNESCO World Heritage Site is truly awe-inspiring. We traveled to Xi’an primarily to see this ancient wonder, and it did not disappoint. **Guides Make All the Difference** If you speak Chinese, **definitely hire an official guide** from the ticket office—their insights bring the history to life in a way that Google or AI simply can’t match. For English speakers, an audio guide (around 40 yuan) is available, though it offers less depth than a live guide. We paid about 90 yuan (+5 yuan per earpiece) for our guide, making it more cost-effective for small groups. **Manage Your Expectations** Even in March (supposedly low season), the site was **packed**. I can’t imagine the crowds in summer—you might struggle to get a clear view of the warriors. Arrive early and be prepared for crowds no matter when you visit. **The Optional XD Experience** After the main tour, guides often recommend an **XD (VR) experience** simulating the emperor’s tomb opening. If you enjoy VR, it’s a fun add-on, but it doesn’t enhance the historical understanding. We skipped it and don’t feel like we missed much. **Final Verdict:** A **must-see** for history buffs, but go with a guide, brace for crowds, and skip the VR unless you’re really into it. The sheer scale and craftsmanship of the Terracotta Army make it worth the visit!
Very cool, go before 10 am, otherwise all the tourgroups will arrive, and spoil the experience a little bit.
One day trip from Beijing with bullet train - enough time to visit museum, enjoy the place and return to Capitol.

This was always a lifelong ambition to visit after hearing about it's discovery back in the early 80s. It simply took my breath away when I visited, the scale of it was simply far larger than I had ever have imagined. Also I had not appreciated that it had been completely destroyed and it is only through what must be a painstaking job, search warrior is now being restored. It is understood that there is another recent discovery of more warriors than what is currently on show, how amazing. Based on advice we arrived early when the facility opened which enabled us to get round and see what we wanted. As soon as the tour groups arrived it became crowded and difficult to see and get photos. To me it was simply amazing and would recommend.

Great museum with intriguing history of China. Recommended to get a tour guide (available in different languages) as there is no poster or text around the museum. We went there in November during the low season so there weren’t many tourists around. There were only squat toilets available for women ( which is common around Xian).
Fascinating place and so much to see, can get a bit crowded and highly recommend a tour guide booked in advance

A really good experience. The museum is well organised and despite 64000 tickets being issued daily, it was easy to get to the displays in the 3 pits. Plenty to do outside the museum too with lots of different food and drink shops. Plenty for souvenir hunters too, don't be afraid to haggle. I got quite a few souvenirs for half of the price they were asking! All together a great day out. I was lucky and got a ticket the day I visited, but I recommend you apply and buy your ticket at least 3 days before you go.

A must see in a lifetime! Such an amazing place to visit - 2000 yrs old history.. a must see truly. Now - to get there and visit properly - you must go on an organised tour. Foreigners cant buy tickets - also not possible on arrival. You have to ask a Chinese national to buy them for you or again go on a bigger tour. You must have your ID with you which is strange for visiting a museum. The crowds are proportionate to the number of people in China so have patience. Security like at the airport.

I've seen the crowds and have read reviews - DO NOT COME IN THE SUMMER hence we decided to visit the place when it was autumn entering into winter. We'd rather it be chilly than brave the throngs of summer people. We hopped on the tourist bus from the Drum Bell Tower for 30 yuan per pax but honestly, taking the Didie is more worth it esp if you're not solo because it's faster and just a few yuans extra (we took Didie on the way back). Prepare to allocate at least 1/2 day for the visit with the to and fro journey. Overall we spent 3 hours in the compound and for me, I felt it wasn't enough. There will be tourist guides bugging you at the entrance, I'm not sure what's the standard price but we paid 100yuan per pax (there were 3 of us), overall, I'm glad we took the guide because there are many interesting infos that she shared with us, not just about the terracotta warriors but China's history & culture too. Stuff that wouldn't be in the audio guide (should you decide to rent one). Pit 1 was the most impressive and massive. You can Google search on where to get the best view of the armies, fortunately for us, it wasn't busy and we were able to see it from all angles from the right side of the entrance (best side). With the guide telling us the story, we were able to understand the formation, uniform, posting, ranking, accessories of the warriors in general. As we moved towards the exit, it was like a journey through time. Next we moved on to Pit 2 and Pit 3 and ending the visit at the newly opened exhibition. We were lucky as it has just been launched 2 months ago. This is where all the information and knowledge regarding the warriors are displayed. Our guide walked us through the important and must see exhibits and skipping those she deemed not too important. After the exit, we enjoyed Bang Biang Noodles, famous in Chang'an/Xi'an. A must try if you want to experience local food but it isn't my cup of tea, unfortunately. I was however surprised that even in tourist areas, they did not hike up the price, kudos. Any advice? - AUTUMN or WINTER would be the best time to visit. The less crowded the better, you can enjoy the exhibit with peace of mind without being pushed around. - Hire a guide and if you have time, do a second round on your own after parting ways with the guide. - A good 3 hours is enough to cover the basics but if you are the type that needs to read everything, add another hour or so (which I wished I did!), the new exhibition is really interesting and amazing, a travelling time machine. Don't miss the immersive show in the end. Must watch! Knock people if you must, get front row seat 😂 Relax and enjoy your visit!

The museum is a bit far from the center of Xian however it’s worth it. We visited in October and it was not crowded , it had some people but it was nice to walk around the museum. We rented the audio tour and it was fine. It was a bit difficult to know which number the pavilion was however you can figure it out. The big pavilion which you see the big statues is amazing . We also bought two statues that was made from the grounds , it is a nice souvenir. It was difficult to find the place to leave the audio guide and nobody speaks English. You have many many restaurantes after leaving the museum.

No doubt one of the great wonders of the world. Perpetually full of people according to a tour guide but avoid China peak holiday season because the crowd is shoulder to shoulder. RMB120 per pax. 4 pits. Some close-up display of the best preserved sculptures in glass. Lots of food places including popular fast foods after exiting the place.

Amazing discovery, worth to visit it. Better go in the afternoon at 14:30 to the Lishan garden, then enter the terra-cotta museum before 16:30. Then you can avoid the crowded time. Recommend to have a guide to tell the stories.

Such an amazing experience. I definitely recommend this visit if you have the time. Everyone is very welcoming. When you walk the expensive area of the historical site you will feel the awe-inspiring aspects of the entire site.

The Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, located in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It houses the Terracotta Army, a massive collection of life-sized terracotta sculptures created over 2,000 years ago to accompany Emperor Qinshihuang in the afterlife. The museum showcases archaeological discoveries, including chariots, weapons, and cultural relics, offering a glimpse into ancient China's history and craftsmanship. Spanning a vast area, the site is considered one of the greatest archaeological finds of the 20th century and a testament to China's rich heritage.

This place is huge. 60Km2 in size (size of Manhatten). The Terracotta Warriors are actually a fair distance from the main burial mound (under Mount Li). Once you have seen pits 1-4 for the Terracotta Warriors, then take a free bus (on left of the entrance if facing it) to go see the bronze chariots (at the base of Mount Li). There, you should pay a little extra for the electric bus as the chariots are a fair walk from the entrance. Avoid going here during public holidays as the crowds will be crazy huge. On Spring Day, there were over 500,000 people! You would spend ALL of your time queuing and never get a chance to even see anything.

Booked private ride and tickets from Klook. The driver arranged for a guide at the area. This place is huge. Recommended to get a guide to help you explore and understand better. Less people after summer holiday.

Ended up taking a 120rmb private car ride from the train station to the site as we could not find the free shuttle bus. Do note that u can easily get Terracotta tickets on WeChat by just inputting any China phone number! Although it was a rainy day, it did not turn away the crowd. Pit 1 was definitely the most spectacular sight! Glad to have witnessed this massive inspirational motivation by the Qin Emperor for his afterlife.

For those interested in history, I highly recommend hiring a guide. The scenery inside is truly impressive. It’s one of those experiences where, although most Chinese children learn about the Terracotta Warriors of the Qin Emperor, seeing them in person is still astonishing. The scale is absolutely massive, far beyond what you can imagine.

Great experience. Together with the Great Wall tells you why was China such great empire, and why it is becoming again. However, it can be a bit crowdy. Official parking available at very enterance, so don't react to many parking offers before. Personal guides with questionable English knoweledge available at enterence. Try to buy souvenires as close to the exit gate as possible, because prices are lower than closer to the exhibition halls.

I really want to give this place five stars. I certainly do not want to discourage anyone from visiting this sacred find, it truly is one of a kind and a national treasure. The traffic between the terracotta soldiers and mosaleum almost non-navigable. We were told about 60,000 people visit each day, wow.

I love this place, the story of how it was doiscovered, the history, the efforts to restore and preserve. It is eye opening to see the wisdom and craftsmanship of past civilizations. A must visit ! Be warned- theres going to be lots of people wanting to see the terracota warriors. Practice patience!

The miracle built over two thousand years ago is definitely worth a visit. It's best to buy tickets in advance. If you hire a tour guide, you can better understand the details and various data of the Terra Cotta Warriors. There are many people selling souvenirs here. If you are very good at bargaining, you can get much cheaper.

I would highly suggest you approach your hotel front desk and ask if there is any day tour (No shopping) available. It might be more worth it if you go with a tour. Booked a day tour via CTrip for CNY288 and opted for a small group one with no more than 8 pax. There are 3 halls here, all built directly above the excavation site. The first was discovered in 1974, by a villager who was digging for a well. On his 3rd attempt, he uncovered many broken 'tiles' and from there, the Terracotta army was found. The entire area is estimated to host over 8000 pcs but so far, only 2000+ are excavated because they still haven't had the technology to preserve the colours on them. Once exposed, these artifacts lose their colour in 3-5 days. Most are found broken into 30 - 100 pieces, it takes anything between 8 months to 2 years to restore each soldier/horse/carriage. What we see today is the result of over 40 years of restoration work, that's still ongoing. Amazing how each of them are unique, with a different expression, hairstyle and even shoes, 千人千面. The only commonality is that they all have single eyelids. Each soldier is mounted on a platform which has cities carved into it, but it's unknown if the cities are where the soldiers are from or where the figurine is made. 秦兵马俑一号坑遗址 is the first and largest site, consisting mainly the frontline soldiers (步兵), the 2nd consists the special forces (特种兵) and the 3rd holds the commanding general and adviser. The 2nd site is largely untouched, but this is where they've displayed 5 exhibits in proper display cases, as this is the location where the only complete piece of soldier (跪射俑) was found. In the 3rd site, they've also left a section as it was (with the broken pieces), as a display for visitors to see how it originally looks, for comparison sake. It is also here that they've recreated a section in a photo studio setting (with proper lighting) where you can pay CNY10 per person to take photos with it on your own camera. The Souvenir store is near to the 3rd location and in there, they sell these mini replicas of the Terracottas, made from the original earth/mud from the excavation site, and comes with certification from the museum, so one can own a real piece of this site.

Upon our arrival at Xian Train Station, we were greeted by our lovely expert local guide, Lucy, who was waiting for us at the arrival gate. We then headed straight on to visit Terracotta Army archaeological site, located at 45 km of Xian. The discovery of the army was in March 1974, by farmers who were digging a water well near Mount Li, where the Emperor Qin Shi Huang tomb is located. The army was built to protect the emperor Qin Shi Huang in the afterlife, and of course to show all his glory, after all, he was the one who united the states, building one of the most dominant empires in China. Upon arrival to the archaeological site, and as I was already expecting, it was crowded, in fact, extremely crowded, so it was very convenient having Lucy’s help, as she had arranged our entry tickets in advance. The terracotta warriors are a true marvel of history, no wonder why its discovery is considered as one of the greatest in the 20th century! I was static at seeing each figure, so meticulously sculpted, each with its unique facial expression, I felt nearly as if they were trying to say something. My imagination went back in time, wondering the moments when they were being sculpted, and also the army of people that surely had to work on them then, their thoughts, their beliefs.. We had time to visit the three pits and managed to survive alive the “walk and push” system to make our way through and observe closely, and also to have some photos taken. However, at times we felt exhausted of the crowds. I could see Felipe was very impressed by the warriors. He stayed staring at them for ages and “fought” his way through by advancing the Chinese way… that is pushing-advancing des-pa-ci-to..and without apologies through the crowd. Pit No.1 contains the majority of the army with over 6000 statues, of those approximately 2000 has been restored or uncovered. This place is great, but in order to fully enjoy it you need to temper your expectations a bit. I have many friends who visited it while in China thinking it would be an incredible and life-changing experience. They wound up all feeling somewhat disappointed by the place. Luckily for me, I had heard all of the things they disliked about it before going, and as a result of my expectations being lowered, my experience there wound up being great. First, the positives: The detail on the warriors is amazing, the scale is incredible, and the historical and cultural significance of this place is almost without parallel in China, let alone the world. There are three buildings to see, but the first building is the one everyone thinks of when they see the warriors, and is far and away the most impressive. It truly is a sight to behold, guaranteed to make you say "wow" out loud the first time you see it (it's a shame the building they are housed in is pretty drab and industrial). Buildings 2 and 3 are newer and are much earlier in the process of excavation and restoration, but they are still absolutely worth a visit in their own right. Now the negatives: The crowds are insane here, even for China. If you haven't lived in China before or spend a considerable amount of time seeing tourist attractions in China, you are going to want to commit murder during the experience. Once the hordes of tourists arrive with their tour guides on loudspeakers waving goofy flags, you will be pushed out of the way so people can take selfies or lift their kids up to get a peek. If you aren't prepared to push yourself or hold your ground, you won't see that much and will leave with a sour taste in your mouth. Forget about seeing the chariots/carriages in the museum, you're lucky if you can get within 15 feet of the enclosure (and there will be about 200 Chinese people in front of you). You will also encounter tons of souvenir sellers trying to pawn off overpriced replica warriors, T-shirts, and other useless trinkets. And once you see building 1, the rest of the place will be somewhat of a let-down. But by tempering your expectations, you can enjoy this place a lot. Leave as early as possible in the morning and get there as the ticket booths open (or before to stake out a place in line). If you arrive anytime after 10:00am, you're going to have a miserable experience. If you have the money, I recommend getting a taxi from Xi'an to the museum, as it avoids the hassle of dealing with a Chinese tour bus (where little to no English will be spoken). Round trip taxi fare with a driver who speaks rudimentary English (a rarity in China) cost only 500 kuai (about $70) even without haggling, and it gets you there when you want to be there. Also, although I'm usually not big on tour guides they can be a lifesaver here, as the walk from the parking area to the ticket office is long and confusing, and they all have friends waiting in line who can help get your tickets faster. Plus they know how to avoid the crowds as much as possible, and the historical perspective they offer is great and welcomed, since there is very little signage or information in most of the areas (especially building 1). Ours cost only 150 kuai (about $22) and was well worth the price. By realizing the above and following some of the advice, it will make your experience better, and you will leave glad that you came.

Accessibility is also a priority, with clear signage and well-maintained pathways that make it easy for everyone to navigate the vast complex. Visiting the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I highly recommend. It’s a place where history comes alive, offering a unique glimpse into the ancient world.
